title: Kolkata's Satyajit Ray film institute stays shut until 11 December as student protests go on
dek: SRFTI extended its campus closure by about a month, citing security; students, protesting since violence at an RSS-linked event in September, want the vice-chancellor to go.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute (SRFTI) in Kolkata has extended the closure of its campus until 11 December, keeping the government-funded film school shut for about two months as students press on with protests that began after violence on campus in late September.

A senior official told reporters on Thursday that the situation had been reviewed "in consultation with deans of both films and EDM", the institute's film and electronic and digital media wings, and the earlier order extended. "We had on October 13 initially suspended film and digital media classes till November 13 but are forced to extend it by about a month," the official said, according to reports. The institute cited the need for security after allegations of intimidation, physical abuse and vandalism, and accused protesting students of continuing to occupy hostels despite being told to leave.

## How it began

The trouble started on 27 September, when an event organised by the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat, an RSS-affiliated consumer group, was held in a campus auditorium. Students objected, and clashes followed in which stones and bottles were thrown; about 30 students and two faculty members were reportedly injured. On 4 October members of the Bangiya Hindu Jagaran Mancha threw bricks, stones and bottles at students from outside the main gate, according to reports. That evening students surrounded Vice-Chancellor Santosh Ajmera in his office for about five hours and demanded his resignation.

On 15 October a Dean's Council recommended rusticating six students it regarded as leaders of the agitation; one of the charges was "manhandling" the vice-chancellor on 4 October. Students deny violence but have acknowledged pushing and shoving and intemperate language, according to reports. Academic activities were suspended on 16 October, during the Durga Puja break, and students were told to vacate hostels within 24 hours. Police have been stationed on the campus since late October; the administration says only four or five personnel are there.

A fact-finding committee of the institute and a separate state government inquiry involving senior police officers were set up, reports said. Their findings have not been published.

## What each side says

Students say the administration is "collectively punishing" them. In a statement titled "How long will this administrative failure continue?", they said they had been deprived of food, drinking water, electricity and Wi-Fi during the suspension and demanded accountability and a return to normal academic life, according to reports. They say a faculty member received a show-cause notice for helping the cinematographer Ranjan Palit enter the campus for a workshop, that two contractual faculty members were dismissed and that the services of five resource persons were ended.

Their demands include accountability for the September violence, the vice-chancellor's resignation, withdrawal of the rustication orders, removal of police from the campus and restoration of hostel and mess facilities. On 28 October, 31 faculty members asked Mr Ajmera to restore hostel facilities in full and remove the police, reports said.

The administration says a small group of students is being driven by outsiders. Mr Ajmera, an Indian Information Service officer who took charge two days before the 27 September event, said on 27 October that the protest had been "turned into a platform for political and ideological battles, with demands that went beyond the institution's jurisdiction", according to reports. An official said this week that a handful of students were driven by "outside elements and politicising the issue". Administration members have noted that permission for the 27 September event was given before Mr Ajmera arrived.

Filmmakers including Naseeruddin Shah, Saeed Akhtar Mirza and Payal Kapadia have backed the students, reports said.

## What happens next

Classes are not due to resume before 11 December. Students have said they will keep protesting until the vice-chancellor goes, and the results of the two inquiries are awaited. No public statement on the closure from the central government had been reported by Friday.
